turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: I don't really know, honestly. Mostly I just... I don't feel like myself anymore. I used to be out all the time, you know? I stopped hiking, stopped coaching the little league team. My guitar is just gathering dust in the corner. I used to play a lot of classic rock, Zeppelin, Sabbath, that kind of stuff. I had this really nice Gibson Les Paul, cherry sunburst, but I had to sell it a few years back when the transmission went out on my truck. That truck was a nightmare, always something wrong with it. Anyway, I don't even call people back anymore. Some days I just sit in my small rental for hours. I know there are things I should be doing, dishes, laundry, but I just... I can't make myself start. turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had periods where you felt the opposite—unusually energetic, wired, or needing very little sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Wired? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm just tired all the time now. I used to pull some really long shifts, though. When you work protective services, sometimes you're on a perimeter watch for twelve, fourteen hours straight. You have to stay awake, but it's not because you're energetic, you know? You just drink a lot of coffee. We used to get our coffee from this little 24-hour diner down the street from the industrial site. The guy who ran it, Sal, he made the absolute worst coffee. Tasted like battery acid and burnt plastic. 

But he had these amazing cherry pies in the rotating display case. The glass on the case was always smudged, though. People pointing at the pies, leaving their greasy fingerprints all over the glass. I really hate fingerprints on glass. When I clean my windows, I always use newspaper instead of paper towels. The ink acts like a mild abrasive or something, it leaves absolutely no streaks. My grandfather taught me that trick. He used to read the Sunday paper cover to cover, every single section, and then we'd use it to wash his old Buick. It was a LeSabre, powder blue. You don't see cars in that color anymore. Everything now is just silver or black or white. It's really boring, honestly, driving down the highway and seeing the exact same three colors over and over.

turns.doctor_question: Before things started unraveling after your divorce, had you ever gone through a period where you felt this down or lost interest in things?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't... I don't think I ever felt this empty before. Even when things were hard, you know? Like when I first started out in protective services, the training was brutal. They really push you to your limits, physically and mentally. We had to run these obstacle courses in full gear, in the middle of July. The heat radiating off the asphalt was just... it was suffocating. You could see the heat waves distorting the air, making everything look wavy, like you were underwater. 

I actually almost drowned once when I was a kid. My family went to this lake up north, Lake Winnipesaukee, I think it was. We had rented this little pontoon boat for the week. The seats were covered in that cheap vinyl that gets scorching hot in the sun and sticks to the back of your legs when you stand up. My dad had this old cooler, one of those heavy metal Coleman ones, painted green. He always filled it with ice and these little glass bottles of root beer. You had to use a bottle opener to get the caps off. I used to collect the bottle caps, actually. I had a whole shoebox full of them under my bed. I sorted them by brand and color. The orange crush ones were my favorite because the orange was so bright. I wonder whatever happened to that shoebox... probably got thrown out when my mom redecorated my room. She painted the walls this awful shade of yellow, like mustard. Who paints a bedroom mustard yellow? It's supposed to be a relaxing space, you know? Not a hot dog stand.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from work training to heat, drowning, a boat, a cooler, bottle caps, and finally room paint.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient states they have never felt 'this empty before,' indicating they are currently experiencing a profound sense of emptiness.

turns.doctor_question: How has your sleep been over these past several months?
turns.patient_response:
Sleep? It's... well, I don't really know how to describe it. I guess I'm not sleeping much. Or maybe I am, but it doesn't feel like it. I just lie there, staring at the ceiling. The ceiling in this rental has that popcorn texture, you know? The kind they used to put in houses back in the seventies or eighties. It's supposed to help with acoustics, I think, or maybe just to hide imperfections in the drywall. But if you look at it long enough, the shadows from the streetlights make the little bumps look like a map. Like tiny mountain ranges and valleys. 

I used to love looking at maps when I was younger. Real maps, the paper kind that you fold up, not the ones on a phone. My uncle had this massive atlas in his study. It was bound in this dark red leather, smelled like old paper and pipe tobacco. He smoked a cherry blend, which always made the room smell sweet. He had a pipe stand on his desk carved out of walnut wood. It held three pipes, but he only ever used two of them. The third one was just decorative, I think. It had this intricate carving of a ship on the bowl. A galleon, maybe, with the sails fully unfurled. I always wanted to learn how to sail, actually. Getting out on the open water, just the wind and the waves. But I get seasick so easily. Even just standing on a dock if the water is a little choppy makes my stomach turn. Have you ever tried those motion sickness wristbands? The ones with the little plastic bead that presses into your wrist? I bought a pair once before a deep-sea fishing trip, but I lost one of them in the parking lot before we even got on the boat.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits marked tangentiality, drifting from the topic of sleep to ceiling textures, maps, an uncle's pipe, sailing, and motion sickness wristbands without returning to the original point.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient reports not sleeping much and lying awake staring at the ceiling, indicating difficulty with sleep.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight over these past months?
turns.patient_response:
Appetite? I mean, I don't really know. I guess I'm not eating as much. Food just doesn't taste like anything right now. It's like chewing cardboard. I used to save all my cardboard boxes, actually. Whenever I'd order something online or get a package, I'd break the boxes down and stack them in the garage. I always thought, you know, what if I need to move? Or what if I need to ship something big? But then they just sit there, taking up space, and the silverfish get into them. Silverfish are so gross. They move so fast when you turn the light on, just scurrying into the cracks. 

My ex-wife hated bugs. Any kind of bug. If she saw a spider, she'd scream like someone was breaking into the house. I always had to be the one to catch them and put them outside. I never liked killing them. Spiders are actually really good for the environment, they eat the mosquitoes and the gnats. We had this huge oak tree in our front yard at the old house, and in the summer, the gnats would just swarm around it like a cloud. You couldn't even walk to the mailbox without breathing them in. The mailbox was one of those heavy cast-iron ones, shaped like a little barn. The flag on the side was painted red, but the paint was chipping off. I kept meaning to repaint it, maybe a bright cherry red, but I never got around to it. You know how it is, you make these lists of projects for the weekend, and then Saturday rolls around and you just want to sit on the porch. The porch had these great wooden rocking chairs. They squeaked a little when you rocked, but it was a nice sound. Like a metronome.

symptom_reasoning.S026: The patient reports a decrease in appetite, noting they are not eating as much and that food has lost its taste.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any thoughts of wanting to end your life or wishing you were dead?
turns.patient_response:
Dead? I mean... no, not really. I don't sit around thinking about ending it all. It's more like I just want the noise to stop. But dead... no. I did go to a funeral once, though. Last year, I think. My great-aunt Martha passed away. She was ninety-two, lived a long life. They had the service at this old church downtown, the one with the huge stained-glass windows. The colors in those windows were incredible, especially when the sun hit them just right. The blue glass looked like the deep ocean. 

I always wanted to go scuba diving in the ocean. See the coral reefs before they all die off. I watched this documentary once about the Great Barrier Reef, and the fish were just... neon. Like someone painted them with highlighters. I used to use highlighters all the time when I was studying for my protective services exams. Yellow, pink, green. I had this system where yellow was for general concepts, pink was for important dates, and green was for the legal codes. I had this whole pencil case full of them. It was made of that clear plastic, so you could see everything inside. It got a crack in the corner, though, and the zipper kept getting stuck. Zippers are so frustrating when they get stuck. You try to pull them back and forth, and they just bite harder into the fabric. I had a winter coat like that once, a heavy parka. The zipper jammed right when it was ten degrees outside, and I had to walk all the way to my car shivering. My car heater took forever to warm up, too. It was an old sedan, maroon. Maroon is a weird color for a car, don't you think? It's like it wants to be red, but it's too tired.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from a funeral to stained glass, the ocean, scuba diving, highlighters, zippers, and finally a car's color.
symptom_reasoning.S032: The patient explicitly denies having thoughts of ending their life or wishing they were dead.

turns.patient_response:
The noise? Yeah... well, it's like my scanner. You know, from work. Even when I make sure the power is totally off, I still hear these short, radio-like voices coming through. Just bursts of sound. They usually warn me, telling me that someone is inside the house, or that I'm being watched. Being watched is... well, you have to stay vigilant. That's why I always buy the lithium batteries for my gear. The alkaline ones always leak if you leave them in too long. Have you ever had to clean up battery acid? It gets all crusty and white, and it completely ruins the metal contacts. You have to use an old toothbrush and some baking soda to scrub it off. I usually buy those multipacks of toothbrushes at the pharmacy, the ones with the rubber grips on the handle. They just feel better in your hand, you know? They don't slip if your hands are wet. 

But anyway, because of the radio voices, I'll go and clear every room in the house. Standard procedure, checking the closets, behind the doors, making sure the perimeter is secure. But even after I've cleared every single room and I know the place is completely empty, I'll still sometimes see this shadow move right past the hallway. Just darting by. The hallway doesn't even have any windows, so it really shouldn't have shadows moving like that. I actually wanted to put a skylight in there once. Let some natural light in. Skylights always seem like a really good idea until they start leaking when it rains. My neighbor had one, and it ruined his ceiling. Then you're up on the roof with a bucket of tar and a trowel in the middle of a thunderstorm. Roof tar smells awful, like burning tires. It sticks to your boots, too, and you end up tracking it all over the carpet.

turns.doctor_question: Did you ever hear those voices or see those shadows before you began feeling down after your divorce?
turns.patient_response: Before? No, I don't think so. It's been about four months now, the voices and the shadows, and just this constant feeling that people are tracking me. Four months. That's a third of a year. It's funny how we divide time up like that, isn't it? Quarters, thirds, halves. Like slicing up a pie. I used to love cherry pie. My grandmother made the best cherry pie from scratch. She'd spend hours pitting the cherries by hand, and her fingers would be stained red for days afterward. She had this little metal tool for it, a cherry pitter. It looked almost like a hole puncher. Hole punchers are so satisfying to use, the way they snap through the paper and leave those little white circles everywhere. They look like confetti. I bought confetti for a New Year's Eve party once, back when we lived in the apartment. It was metallic, gold and silver stars. They got stuck in the carpet fibers, and I was still vacuuming them up in July. Vacuums are so loud, though. The motor just screams. I had to buy earplugs to use mine. The foam ones that you roll up between your fingers and then they expand in your ear. They're orange, usually. Neon orange, like traffic cones. You see those everywhere during construction season, lined up on the highway. People always knock them over.

turns.doctor_question: During these past four months when you've heard the voices and felt watched, was there ever a time when your mood felt completely back to normal?
turns.patient_response: Normal? No... no, I haven't felt normal at all. Not for a single day since this all started. It's just been a constant weight, you know? A weight. Like carrying around a heavy rucksack. We used to do these training exercises where we had to ruck for miles with fifty pounds on our backs. You really feel it in your knees after a while. The cartilage just wears down. My uncle had to get both of his knees replaced. Titanium joints. It's amazing what they can do with metal these days, putting it right into the body. Titanium is so light, though. They use it for airplanes and golf clubs. I tried golfing once, but I could never get the swing right. It's all in the hips, they say, but I always ended up slicing the ball into the woods. The woods are so quiet, though. Well, except for the birds. I used to have a bird feeder, but the squirrels always figured out how to climb the pole and steal the seeds. They're clever little things. They have these sharp claws that can grip onto anything. I bought this special baffle to put on the pole, like a big plastic dome, but they just jumped from the nearest tree right onto it. Trees are getting so expensive to take down, too. My neighbor had an oak tree removed and it cost him thousands. The stump grinder was massive, looked like some kind of medieval torture device. It just chewed the wood into sawdust. Sawdust smells really good, though, like fresh pine. I love the smell of pine. It reminds me of those little air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. The green ones shaped like trees. They always lose their scent after a week, though. You end up just leaving it there for years until it fades out to a pale, dusty color. Dusty... yeah, no, my mood hasn't been normal at all. Just heavy.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from a heavy rucksack to knee replacements, titanium, golf, squirrels, and stump grinders before finally returning to the topic of their mood.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes their mood as a 'constant weight' and 'heavy', stating they haven't felt normal for a single day since it started.
